parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the accuracy of a measured value.

markscheme_points.text: how close the (measured) value is to the true value (of the quantity)

hints: Hint 1: Think about the word true - accuracy is not about getting the same reading again and again, it is about getting close to what the value really should be.
parts.proper_answer: Accuracy is how close a measured value is to the true value of the quantity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Separate accuracy from precision**
It is easy to mix these up, so let us fix it. Precision is about repeatability and small spread. Accuracy is different. Imagine aiming at a target. You are accurate when your hits land close to the bullseye, which is the true value.

Step 2: **State the definition**
So accuracy means closeness to the true value. A measurement can be precise but not accurate if there is a systematic error shifting all readings away from the true value.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
Two solid cubes, A and B, are measured to determine the density of their materials.

Table 1.1 shows the measurements for cube A.

Table 1.1

| quantity | measurement |
| length of side | $(1.53 \pm 0.01 \text{ cm})$ |
| mass | $(31.3 \pm 0.5 \text{ g})$ |
parts.text: Show that the calculated density of the material of cube A is $8.7 \times 10^{3} \text{ kg m}^{-3}$.
hints: Hint 1: Start from the shape. You have the side length of a cube, so think how you get its volume from one side, and check what units the final density needs to be in.
Hint 2: Use $\rho = m/V$ with mass in kg and side in m, then cube the side to get $V$ in $\text{m}^3$ before dividing.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Get mass and volume in SI units**
Density links how much matter is packed into a space. For a cube, $$V = l^3$$ Convert first: $$m = 31.3\text{ g} = 31.3 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kg}$$ $$l = 1.53\text{ cm} = 1.53 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$$

Step 2: **Calculate density**
Now use: $$\rho = \frac{m}{V} = \frac{m}{l^3}$$ $$\rho = \frac{31.3 \times 10^{-3}}{(1.53 \times 10^{-2})^3}$$ $$(1.53 \times 10^{-2})^3 = 3.58 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^3$$ $$\rho = 8.74 \times 10^3\text{ kg m}^{-3} \approx 8.7 \times 10^3\text{ kg m}^{-3}$$ This shows the required result.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the density of the material of cube A.
hints: Hint 1: Think about which operations magnify uncertainty. Adding or multiplying by a power does not treat uncertainty the same way - a cubed length will contribute more than a single mass reading.
Hint 2: Add the % uncertainty in mass to three times the % uncertainty in side length: $(0.5/31.3)\times 100 + 3\times(0.01/1.53)\times 100$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Write the rule for $\rho = m/l^3$**
When you multiply or divide, you add percentage uncertainties. When you raise to a power, you multiply the percentage uncertainty by that power. Here: $$\frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} \times 100 = \frac{\Delta m}{m} \times 100 + 3 \times \frac{\Delta l}{l} \times 100$$ The factor 3 is the key point because $V = l^3$.

Step 2: **Put in the numbers**
$$\frac{\Delta m}{m} \times 100 = \frac{0.5}{31.3} \times 100 = 1.60\%$$ $$\frac{\Delta l}{l} \times 100 = \frac{0.01}{1.53} \times 100 = 0.65\%$$ $$\text{uncertainty in density} = 1.60 + 3 \times 0.65 = 1.60 + 1.96 = 3.56\%$$ This is about $4\%$. So $\rho_A = 8.7 \times 10^3\text{ kg m}^{-3} \pm 4\%$.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text:
The density of the material of cube B is determined to be $9.2 \times 10^{3} \text{ kg m}^{-3} \pm 6\%$.

State and explain whether cube A and cube B could be made from the same material.

markscheme_points.text: The ranges (of the densities of A and B) overlap or the (calculated) density of A is within the range of the density of B or the difference in densities is within the uncertainty (of B)

hints: Hint 1: Do not just compare 8.7 and 9.2 directly. Think about the spread each value could really lie in once its $\%$ uncertainty is applied.
Hint 2: Work out the lowest and highest possible density for A and for B and see if those two intervals share any common values.
parts.proper_answer: Yes, they could be the same material because the uncertainty ranges overlap. Cube A is $8.7 \times 10^3 \text{ kg m}^{-3} \pm 4\%$ and cube B is $9.2 \times 10^3 \text{ kg m}^{-3} \pm 6\%$, so the value for A lies within the range for B.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the possible ranges**
Let us turn the $\%$ into real limits. For A: $$4\% \text{ of } 8.7 \times 10^3 \approx 0.35 \times 10^3$$ So A lies roughly from $8.35 \times 10^3$ to $9.05 \times 10^3\text{ kg m}^{-3}$. For B: $$6\% \text{ of } 9.2 \times 10^3 \approx 0.55 \times 10^3$$ So B lies roughly from $8.65 \times 10^3$ to $9.75 \times 10^3\text{ kg m}^{-3}$.

Step 2: **Decide if same material is possible**
The two intervals overlap between about $8.65$ and $9.05 \times 10^3\text{ kg m}^{-3}$. The difference between $8.7$ and $9.2$ is smaller than the combined uncertainty. That means the difference could be due to measurement uncertainty alone, so yes, they could be made from the same material.
